How the LoloBuy buying flow works.

A practical, fact-led guide to the product-link, warehouse and international-parcel process.

Buying guide · 8 minute read

From a product link to an international parcel: a clear way to evaluate each step

People often search for a LoloBuy spreadsheet because they want a faster route from a product idea to a product page. A spreadsheet can be useful for discovery, but it does not replace the checks that matter after you find an item. The practical process is a sequence of decisions: find an item, review the listing, submit the order, wait for the seller to send it to the warehouse, examine the information that becomes available, then decide whether and how to send a parcel internationally. Keeping these steps separate avoids the common mistake of treating a product link as a completed international order.

1. Start with a specific item, not a vague search

The LoloBuy flow begins with an item link from a supported Chinese marketplace. Before submitting it, read the active listing closely. Check the variant, size, colour, quantity and seller information. Screenshots and product titles can be incomplete or old; the active listing is where options and price changes normally appear. If a spreadsheet helped you discover an item, use it as a starting point, then compare it with the original listing before you pay. This is especially important for clothing and footwear, where one name can contain several versions with different sizing or materials.

Make a simple note of what you expect to receive: for example, black, medium, one unit and a specific version. This makes QC review more useful later because you are not relying on a thumbnail or memory. It also keeps a product decision separate from a shipping decision. At this stage you are choosing an item, not yet choosing an international parcel.

2. Understand the two shipping stages

After an order is submitted, the marketplace seller first sends the item domestically to the LoloBuy warehouse in China. This is distinct from the international shipment to your address. The two stages can move at different speeds because different parties control them: the seller controls domestic dispatch, while international choices become relevant after the warehouse receives the item. That distinction makes status updates easier to understand and prevents unrealistic expectations when a seller has not dispatched yet.

Once the warehouse has the item, it can be stored while you decide what else belongs in the same parcel. Consolidation is not automatically the best choice for every buyer. It can reduce the number of separate parcels, but the useful choice depends on the items, their size, their weight, destination rules and the shipping options currently presented for that destination. Do not treat a community estimate as a promise. The checkout information shown for your own parcel is more relevant than a screenshot from another country or another month.

3. Use QC information as a decision tool

When QC information or photos are available, use them to answer focused questions rather than asking whether an item looks good in general. Compare visible colour, logo placement, construction, measurements when supplied and the product variant with the note you made earlier. QC images can show what has arrived at the warehouse, but they do not guarantee product quality, durability, authenticity, fit or delivery outcome. They are one source of evidence, not a replacement for judgement.

If you ask a community for a second opinion, share only images that do not expose personal information. Do not publish order IDs, parcel IDs, full tracking numbers, addresses, payment screenshots or account details. A useful question names the feature you want checked, such as a size label, a visible mark or a colour difference. Vague questions tend to produce vague answers, while a clear comparison can help you decide whether to continue, seek support or choose another item.

4. Build a parcel deliberately

Before submitting an international parcel, review what is inside it. Consider item type, packaging, total dimensions and destination-country restrictions. Large boxes, fragile items, batteries and restricted goods can affect the options that appear. The correct choice is not simply the cheapest line in an old screenshot. It is the line currently available for your destination and parcel after you have read its conditions. Availability, prices, processing times and carrier choices can change, so they should never be presented as permanent facts.

For buyers in Europe and North America, the practical questions are similar: does this line currently serve my destination, what does checkout show for this parcel, and what local customs, tax or import rules apply? The platform cannot remove the buyer’s responsibility to understand local rules. If anything is unclear, pause before submitting the parcel and use the support path for account-specific questions. Public discussions are useful for general orientation; they are not the right place to disclose private transaction data.

5. Track the parcel in context

After international dispatch, tracking becomes the useful record of movement. A tracking event can indicate a handover, transit stage, customs stage or final delivery activity, but it does not provide a universal delivery estimate. Delays can be caused by carrier handling, capacity, destination processing, customs or missing information. Compare the latest status with the route and destination rather than assuming an update pattern from another parcel will repeat exactly for yours.

If you need help, keep the description concise: destination country, current order or parcel stage, shipping line if shown, approximate time since the last update and the exact non-sensitive status message. Leave out personal identifiers. This makes it easier for support or a community reader to understand the issue without creating a security risk for you.

6. What a useful spreadsheet should do

A good discovery spreadsheet should shorten research, not pressure a purchase. It should lead you to a relevant product category, help you compare options and encourage you to open the live product information. That is why this site sends category and database actions to FindSpreadsheet instead of copying claims from sellers. Use category pages to narrow your search, then use the live database and the original listing to decide whether an item deserves the next step.

The key principle is simple: verify each decision where it belongs. Verify the item on its listing, verify warehouse information when it arrives, verify shipping choices at parcel submission and verify tracking after dispatch. This approach is slower than clicking the first attractive link, but it is much more useful for buyers who want clear evidence instead of guesses.
